summary:
This lunar salvage and base-repair simulator, developed by students of Mazen School, Islamabad, for the 2026 NASA International Space Apps Challenge, challenges players to repair a malfunctioning Moon base by recovering abandoned hardware left behind by past lunar missions—such as historic Apollo-era rovers and landers.

Players begin inside a damaged lunar habitat where an onboard guide system briefs them on the technical specs and history of scattered legacy spacecraft parts. Venturing out onto the 3D lunar surface to locate and salvage each component, players must pass a high-stakes diagnostic quiz upon reaching a part. Answering every question correctly unlocks the hardware so it can be carried back to repair the base—while even a single wrong answer locks the component down and halts mission progress, rewarding careful study before stepping outside.

Built with open-source NASA lunar mission data, the team developed and deployed the browser-based 3D game using Google Gemini (mission logic and quiz design), Google AI Studio & Three.js (3D lunar environment), GitHub (version control), and Netlify (cloud deployment)—turning real space-exploration history and In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) into an engaging educational challenge.
details:
This lunar salvage and base-repair simulator is an interactive 3D educational game developed by students of Mazen School, Islamabad, for the 2026 NASA International Space Apps Challenge. Inspired by real concepts of lunar surface sustainability and In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU), the software places players inside a malfunctioning Moon base where survival depends on studying, locating, and recovering abandoned hardware left behind by past lunar missions—such as historic Apollo rovers, landers, and surface instruments.

What It Does & How It Works

The game combines 3D lunar surface exploration with a strict study-and-verify diagnostic mechanic. Players complete a four-step mission loop to restore their habitat:

  1. Base Briefing & Component Study: Players spawn inside a damaged lunar habitat facing critical technical failures. Before exiting the airlock, the base’s onboard guidance terminal introduces the abandoned spacecraft parts scattered across the Moon, teaching players their historical mission background, engineering specs, and repair functions.
  2. Extravehicular Activity (EVA) Exploration: Players step outside the base onto the 3D lunar surface to locate the legacy hardware resting across craters and plains.
  3. Zero-Margin Diagnostic Quiz: Upon reaching an abandoned space part, the system triggers a technical verification quiz based on the earlier base briefing. Answering every question correctly unlocks the component; however, getting even a single answer wrong keeps the part locked and prevents the player from returning it to advance the mission—reinforcing careful preparation over trial-and-error guessing.
  4. Salvage & Habitat Restoration: Once unlocked, players haul the recovered part back to the base to repair damaged subsystems and restore full habitat operations.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Active Recall & Deep Learning: By tying mission progression directly to a zero-margin quiz, players actively read, retain, and apply real aerospace engineering facts rather than clicking through text without absorbing it.
  • Promotes Space Sustainability & Reuse: Introduces players to the real-world challenge of lunar debris and how future Artemis astronauts could repurpose legacy hardware on the Moon instead of relying entirely on costly resupply launches from Earth.
  • Intended Impact: The project aims to make space history and hardware engineering engaging for students and the public, while demonstrating how young innovators can transform open-source NASA mission archives into interactive, browser-based learning simulations.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Data & Research: Open-source NASA Space Apps Challenge datasets and mission archives detailing Apollo-era lunar surface artifacts, rover components, and habitat life-support subsystems.
  • AI & Prompt Engineering: Google Gemini to structure the salvage mission loop, draft accurate engineering quiz questions, and engineer modular development prompts.
  • 3D Engine & Frontend Stack: Google AI Studio to build the standalone interactive 3D web application using HTML5, CSS3, Tailwind CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js (WebGL).
  • Version Control & Cloud Hosting: GitHub for source-code management and collaborative iteration, paired with Netlify for instant cloud deployment and live browser access during hackathon demonstrations.
  • Hardware Setup: Developed and tested on student laptops (such as HP ProBooks) and designed to run smoothly across standard laptops, tablets, and classroom computers.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered by the Team

  • Turning Past Missions into Gameplay Objectives: Rather than inventing fictional sci-fi items, the team creatively grounded the salvage loop in real abandoned lunar hardware—connecting space history directly to modern survival mechanics.
  • Consequence-Driven Learning Design: The team specifically considered how players often skip educational prompts in games. By designing a strict one-strike quiz lock on each component, they made studying inside the base essential to advancing the mission.
  • Clear Habitat-to-Surface Guidance: Structured the base terminal’s pre-mission briefings so every question encountered on the lunar surface is fair, clear, and directly solvable from the guidance provided inside the habitat.
